result:
Neither five nor ten. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results.

Every agent you add is another model running its own loop, and each one re-reads instructions and passes messages to the others. Anthropic's engineering team reports that agents use about 4× the tokens of a plain chat, and multi-agent systems about 15×. Your sponsor gave you a small budget, so that cost is a real constraint. More agents also means more handoffs where information can get lost or misread.

Anthropic found multi-agent setups paid off for a research tool: lots of work that can run in parallel, more information than fits in one context window, and many complex tools. In their internal tests, a multi-agent version beat a single agent by 90.2%. That was their own eval on open-ended research, not a benchmark of makerspace bookings.

Look at your assistant. It answers from manuals, checks a calendar and books time. That's three tools and mostly sequential steps. A single agent with well-described tools, plus a fixed workflow for steps that never change, will probably do the job. For the review, a defensible starting point is one agent. Split off a second only when you can name the specific problem it solves, such as the manuals flooding the context.

A concrete test: a student asks, "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday at 3?" Which parts of that request could run in parallel, and which have to wait for an earlier result?

I haven't read Anthropic's full post, only search results that quote it. The source is [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system). I can write a lesson on workflows versus agents versus multi-agent systems if you'd like one.

Sources:
- [Engineering at Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
